extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of philosophy and classics interested in Plato's Republic
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze and interpret the passage from Plato's Republic describing the origins, character, and consequences of the tyrannical soul and the hierarchy of pleasures and states. Useful for close reading, philosophical commentary, or teaching notes on Book VIII–IX themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-part soul classification
rubrics_metrics.description: The soul is divided into three principles: the rational (lover of wisdom), the spirited/contentious (lover of honour), and the appetitive (money-loving, desiring bodily pleasures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each part corresponds to a class of men and a distinct set of pleasures and desires; recognising these three parts is the basis for diagnosing character-types (philosopher, soldier, money-maker) and their proper ordering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure hierarchy (rational over bodily)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures of the rational part of the soul (knowledge/truth) are the truest and most genuine; bodily and acquisitive pleasures are shadows and less real.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The philosopher, who pursues truth, experiences pleasures of greater 'being' and so judges truer pleasures; bodily pleasures are transient, often mixed with pain, and less satisfying in reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience, wisdom, and reason as the criterion of true pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience combined with wisdom and reason is the best judge for determining which pleasures are genuine and most desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the philosopher has experience of other pleasures and the faculty of reason, his judgment about pleasures is more authoritative than that of the money-lover or honor-lover; use experience+reason to evaluate competing claims about what is pleasant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as harmony of soul parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice within the individual means each part of the soul doing its own work (no part usurping another); when the whole soul follows the philosophical principle, the parts are just and enjoy their true pleasures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A just soul yields the best life because the parts are ordered properly under reason; injustice is a disordered soul where appetites or spirited elements rule and corrupt pleasures follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tyrannical soul: origin and markers
rubrics_metrics.description: The tyrannical man is generated when lawless desires take hold (especially a master-passion such as erotic love), banishing temperance and reason and admitting madness as captain; he is characterized by insatiable desires, enslavement to passions, and the overthrow of better principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs include domination by a single ruling passion, pursuit of lawless pleasures, moral degradation (theft, violence, false witness), and the replacement of earlier temperate convictions with tyrannical appetites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral indicators of tyranny (social consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tyrannical persons engage in feasts, carousals, reckless deeds, theft, temple plundering, violence, flattery of the vile, informing, and betrayal; when numerous, they form a base that produces public tyrants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for patterns of social depravity and criminality, the creation of retainers/mercenaries, and the seizure of power by the most tyrannical among the depraved as indicators that individual vice has become political tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tyrant's misery compared to other regimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite outward appearances of power, the tyrant is the most miserable: enslaved by fears, jealousy, convulsions, and the need for flattery; he is poorer in soul and never free or friendful like the king/royal man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge a regime or ruler's well-being not by external power but by inner freedom, fearlessness, justice, and harmony: the royal/kingly life is happiest; the tyrannical life is most miserable.

rubrics_metrics.name: False pleasures as reliefs of pain
rubrics_metrics.description: Many intense bodily pleasures are merely reliefs from antecedent pains (hunger, thirst) and thus are not pure pleasures; equating the absence of pain with true pleasure is a common error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples (sickness → relief; appetite satisfaction) to distinguish between true positive pleasures and merely comparative or temporary reliefs; beware treating neutral/rest states as equivalent to genuine pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure pleasures that have no antecedent pain
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist pleasures (e.g., pleasures of smell) that arrive and depart without producing preceding pain; such pleasures show that not all pleasure is merely cessation of pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ such examples to undermine the thesis that pleasure is always the absence of pain and to support the claim that some pleasures are immediate and genuine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of true pleasure by degree of 'being' or truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure derived from things that have greater share of pure existence (the invariable, immortal, true — e.g., knowledge, virtue) is more real than pleasure derived from the variable, mortal realm (food, drink, bodily satisfactions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate pleasures and lives by their relation to truth/being: the more a pleasure partakes in lasting truth/knowledge, the more genuinely fulfilling it is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative metaphor for moral distance (proximity to reason/law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness and pleasure can be measured by distance from law and reason: the farther a soul/state is from law/reason (tyranny), the more removed it is from true pleasure (illustrated by the arithmetic metaphor, e.g., 729-times separation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the metaphorical numerical calculation to convey the vast qualitative gulf between just/kingly life and tyrannical life; it is an emphatic rhetorical device, not a literal mathematical test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence between individual soul types and political regimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual soul-types (royal/philosophic, timocratic, oligarchic, democratic, tyrannical) correspond to types of cities/regimes; their relative virtue and happiness map onto each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing political forms, compare the inner constitution of citizens' souls with the structure of the regime; use the parallel to argue about which regimes promote justice and happiness.
